1.note: Can also be read "a city of broad streets"; the next line rhymes on רְחוֹבוֹת (streets). Compare רְחֹבֹת עִיר, Gen 10:11.

2.he: וָשֵׂבֶר. וְאֵין מָזוֹן וָשֶׁבֶר. כִּי אִם יָגוֹן וָשֶׁבֶר
2.note: Three lines end on the same letters שבר: שֵׂבֶר "expectation" (Ps 119:116), שֶׁבֶר "grain" (Gen 42:1), and שֶׁבֶר "breaking, ruin". The play cannot be carried into English.

3.he: וְעַל כֵּן יָצָאתִי לִקְרָאתֶךָ. לְשַׁחֵר פָנֶיךָ וָאֶמְצָאֶךָ
3.note: Word for word the words of the seductress in Prov 7:15: the trickster greets his victim with them.

4.note: Ḥever greets him with a name from Num 1:11 (Avidan son of Gideoni), and the villager corrects him to Avida (Gen 25:4) the Gibeonite. The names differ by one letter, and Gideoni and Gibeoni by one letter too. The Gibeonites (Josh 9) themselves won by a trick.

5.note: הֶאֱדִיב is "to make pine, grieve" (1 Sam 2:33). There may be a play on אדם "to be red": the heat browned them. Uncertain.

6.note: Isa 50:11 "you shall lie down in sorrow". Bent to the meat laid down to rest after cooking; the exact image is uncertain.

7.note: The form בְּדֹלָחִם is unusual ("crystal", from בְּדֹלַח, perhaps "their crystal"). The words come from Lam 4:7, which the next lines quote (ruddy, pearls, sapphire, cut).

8.note: A pun: שְׁנֵינוּ "both of us" and שִׁנֵּינוּ "our teeth"; the pair comes back in lines 162–163.

9.note: Read צִיר as "pang, pain" (Isa 13:8) and חבשׁ as "bind up" a wound: the sweets heal every pain. צִיר can also mean "envoy" or "hinge"; uncertain.

10.note: Amos 6:4 "beds of ivory"; שֵׁן also means "tooth", so the sweet lies on a bed of teeth.

12.note: מַצֵּבָה is usually "pillar"; here perhaps the stall or raised seat where they ate, or "the station" (מַצָּב). Uncertain.

13.note: נָבָל "scoundrel, fool", also the name of Nabal (1 Sam 25:25). The word comes back at the start of the poem.

14.note: This passage is missing from the Ben-Yehuda text and is taken from Kaminka's edition (Warsaw 1899, p. 207), unvocalized. It runs from this third line of the villager's poem to the end of the gate (pp. 207–208).

15.note: Ps 58:6, of the snake charmer "who charms charms" (see also Deut 18:11). חֹבֵר and חֲבָרִים are from the same root as Ḥever's name (חֶבֶר).
